answer: Predictive coding, cross-lingual review, audio and video evidence, privilege logging, and sentiment analysis of corporate messaging.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Predictive Coding and Technology-Assisted Review
children.blurb: Predictive coding and technology-assisted review cover the use of machine learning to sort large document collections by relevance, most often in litigation, investigations and regulatory responses.

children.name: Cross-Lingual Discovery
children.blurb: Cross-lingual discovery is the practice of finding, reviewing and producing documents in a legal matter when the material spans more than one language.

children.name: Audio and Video Evidence
children.blurb: Audio and video evidence covers recorded speech, surveillance footage, body camera video, call recordings, voicemail, and meeting captures that become part of a legal matter.

children.name: Automated Privilege Logging
children.blurb: Automated privilege logging is the use of software to identify, describe and list documents withheld from production in litigation because they are protected by attorney client privilege or the work product doctrine.

children.name: Intent and Sentiment in Corporate Communications
children.blurb: Intent and sentiment analysis in corporate communications covers the automated reading of emails, chat logs, memos, and filings to infer what a writer meant and how they felt.

sections.body: E-discovery is the work of finding, sorting and producing documents and other records when an organisation is involved in litigation, an investigation or a regulatory request. Artificial intelligence does the heavy lifting that human review teams once did by hand: classifiers rank documents for relevance, language models group near-duplicates, speech recognition turns recorded calls into searchable text, and clustering surfaces themes across millions of files. In practice this means a small review team can work through a collection that would once have taken hundreds of reviewers, and the ranking scores become the basis for negotiations with the other side about how the review was conducted. The field is not about machines deciding a case, it is about triage, ordering and defensibility, with humans still making the calls that matter.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Predictive coding is the most settled part of the field. Courts and practitioners have largely accepted that a well-documented technology-assisted review can be defensible, and the argument has shifted from whether to use it to how to validate and disclose it. Cross-lingual work is harder than it looks, because machine translation introduces errors that then propagate into relevance decisions, and quality varies sharply by language pair and by the kind of text involved. Audio and video remain the least mature area: transcription is good on clear speech and degrades with accents, crosstalk and poor recordings, and diarisation, the problem of knowing who spoke when, is often the real bottleneck. Privilege logging is still mostly manual because the judgement is legal rather than statistical, and sentiment and intent analysis of corporate messaging is suggestive at best, since tone is not the same as knowledge or wrongdoing. The honest limits are consistent across all of it: models inherit the biases of the material they were trained on, they cannot explain themselves in the way a court may demand, and every result needs a documented, repeatable process behind it.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The section opens with Predictive Coding and Technology-Assisted Review, which is the foundation the rest of the pages build on, covering how classifiers are trained, validated and defended. Cross-Lingual Discovery extends that machinery to multilingual collections and deals with the translation problem that sits between the classifier and the documents. Audio and Video Evidence moves from text to recorded material, covering transcription, speaker identification and the handling of formats that do not behave like documents. Automated Privilege Logging addresses the task of identifying and describing protected material, which is where automation meets a legal judgement that resists it. Intent and Sentiment in Corporate Communications closes the section by looking at what tone and language in internal messaging can and cannot tell an investigator. A reader new to the subject should start with predictive coding, then follow whichever evidence type matches their matter, and treat the sentiment page as a caution about reading too much into style.
